triage.name: Bursitis
triage.reason: Focal joint-region pain and swelling reachable by history, exam and aspiration; good musculoskeletal differential teaching.

demographics: More common in adults who perform repetitive occupational or recreational activities
Occupational groups with frequent kneeling, leaning on elbows, or overhead work are overrepresented

risk_factors.text: Repetitive joint motion or prolonged pressure on a joint (kneeling, leaning on elbows)
Recent direct trauma to the joint region
Occupations or sports requiring repetitive kneeling, throwing, or overhead activity

social_history: Occupations involving repetitive kneeling or elbow leaning (e.g., plumbers, carpet layers, gardeners)
Sports with repetitive overhead or throwing motion

chief_complaints.text: My knee hurts and looks swollen
It hurts when I move my elbow
There's a tender lump near my joint

hpi.onset: Gradual over days, often after a period of increased repetitive activity or prolonged pressure on the joint
hpi.progression: Pain and swelling build up gradually; may improve with rest but recur with activity
hpi.location: Over the affected bursa — most often the prepatellar or olecranon region, but can occur at the shoulder, hip, or heel
hpi.radiation: Usually local; pain may spread along the adjacent muscle with movement
hpi.quality: Aching, sore, and tender; sharp with specific movements or pressure
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; 3–6/10 at rest, worse with movement
hpi.timing: Worse with activity and direct pressure; better with rest
aggravating: Kneeling or leaning on the elbow
Stair climbing or squatting (for knee bursitis)

associated_symptoms.text: Stiffness or limited range of motion
Mild redness of the overlying skin

pertinent_negatives: Joint redness and severe pain at rest suggesting infection
Recent penetrating injury or open wound over the joint
Systemic symptoms such as weight loss or night sweats
Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

negatives: Locking or catching of the joint
argues_against: True joint line tenderness with locking

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with less swelling and more chronic pain, often confused with osteoarthritis; slower recovery.
Higher risk of septic bursitis and slower healing; may have less obvious inflammatory signs.
Increased mechanical stress on weight-bearing joints; may have more diffuse pain and difficulty localizing to the bursa.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, no distress, moves the limb with mild discomfort
general.moderate: Mild distress with movement, splints or guards the affected joint
general.severe: Ill-appearing with marked focal swelling, reluctant to move the joint
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, febrile, diaphoretic, holding the limb still

findings.maneuver: Palpate directly over the affected bursa (prepatellar, olecranon, or other site)
findings.finding: Well-localized tenderness directly over the bursa

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the affected joint region
findings.finding: Localized swelling or fluctuant fullness over the bursa

findings.maneuver: Assess skin temperature over the swollen area
Inspect the skin overlying the bursa
findings.finding: Mild erythema over the swollen area

findings.maneuver: Passively and actively move the affected joint through its range
findings.finding: Pain with movement, especially at end range, without true joint-line tenderness

findings.maneuver: Stress the joint ligaments and assess for instability
findings.finding: No ligamentous laxity or joint instability

findings.maneuver: Palpate the joint line itself, distinct from the bursa
findings.finding: No tenderness at the joint line

findings.maneuver: Assess for intra-articular effusion (e.g., ballottement or bulge sign at the knee)
Ask the patient to flex and extend the joint while observing for mechanical symptoms
findings.finding: No locking, catching, or giving way

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin surrounding the bursa for spreading erythema, induration, or drainage
findings.finding: No spreading cellulitis, no open wound or draining sinus

findings.maneuver: Observe general appearance and assess for systemic signs of infection
findings.finding: No fever, chills, or toxic appearance

findings.maneuver: Examine other joints for swelling or tenderness

labs.caveat: Mildly elevated in aseptic bursitis; marked elevation favors septic bursitis or another inflammatory process.
Nonspecific; helps gauge inflammation but does not distinguish aseptic from septic bursitis.
Normal in aseptic bursitis; leukocytosis suggests septic bursitis or another systemic process.
Left shift accompanies leukocytosis in septic bursitis.
Hyperglycemia raises concern for septic bursitis and poor healing; check in patients with diabetes.
Consider when gout is in the differential; normal uric acid does not exclude gout.

findings.text: Soft tissue swelling over the bursa
Degenerative joint changes (osteophytes, joint space narrowing) if coexisting osteoarthritis

imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is uncertain or aspiration is planned

findings.text: Distended bursa with fluid and thickened synovial wall
Increased Doppler flow in the bursal wall (hyperemia)
Guidance for diagnostic or therapeutic aspiration

imaging.preferred_when: Persistent symptoms despite treatment or suspicion of a deeper process

findings.text: Bursal fluid collection with surrounding soft tissue edema

initial.why: Rules out fracture, dislocation, or advanced arthritis and shows soft tissue swelling
Baseline inflammatory marker; helps screen for septic bursitis
initial.only_if: fever, marked warmth, or concern for infection

initial.why: Adds to CRP when infection or inflammatory arthritis is considered
initial.only_if: fever, marked warmth, or concern for infection
fever, systemic symptoms, or concern for infection

confirmatory.test: Bursal aspiration with cell count, Gram stain, and culture
confirmatory.why: Distinguishes aseptic from septic bursitis and identifies the organism
confirmatory.only_if: Distinguishes aseptic from septic bursitis and identifies the organism

supporting.why: Confirms bursal fluid and guides aspiration
supporting.only_if: diagnosis is uncertain or aspiration is planned

supporting.why: Defines bursal and adjacent soft tissue involvement
supporting.only_if: symptoms persist despite treatment or a deeper process is suspected

supporting.why: Assesses glycemic control and risk of septic bursitis
Evaluates gout when the presentation is atypical

not_indicated.why: Not needed for typical aseptic bursitis that responds to conservative care
Not routine in afebrile, well-appearing patients with typical bursitis
Not routine in afebrile, well-appearing patients with typical bursitis
Not routine in afebrile, well-appearing patients with typical bursitis

not_indicated.test: Bursal aspiration with cell count, Gram stain, and culture
not_indicated.why: Not routine in afebrile, well-appearing patients with typical aseptic bursitis
No role in focal joint-region swelling
Not needed unless pain is epigastric

decision_points: Aspirate the bursa before injecting steroid when infection is possible
Fever, marked warmth, or overlying cellulitis should prompt aspiration and cultures rather than empiric steroid injection
Persistent symptoms beyond 6 to 12 months despite conservative care warrant orthopedic referral

differential.name: Septic bursitis
differential.why_considered: Inflamed bursa with pain, swelling and warmth; the key distinction from aseptic bursitis
differential.trigger: Fever, marked warmth, overlying cellulitis, or a bursa that is exquisitely tender and rapidly enlarging

history: Fever and chills
Rapid onset over hours to a couple of days
Recent penetrating trauma, skin break, or insect bite over the bursa
Diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression
exam: Marked focal warmth and erythema
Overlying cellulitis or a draining sinus
Severe tenderness limiting even passive movement
Ill appearance or systemic toxicity
labs: Bursal aspirate with high white cell count, low glucose, positive Gram stain or culture
imaging: Ultrasound shows complex or loculated bursal fluid with prominent wall hyperemia
MRI shows marked surrounding soft tissue edema and enhancement

differential.name: Osteoarthritis of the affected joint
differential.why_considered: Chronic joint pain and swelling in the same age group, especially at the knee

history: Gradual onset over months to years
Pain worse with activity and better with rest, but chronic and persistent
Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes
exam: Bony enlargement and crepitus at the joint line
Joint-line tenderness rather than isolated bursal tenderness
Possible intra-articular effusion
Reduced range of motion with mechanical symptoms
labs: Normal inflammatory markers in uncomplicated disease
imaging: Joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts on x-ray

differential.name: Gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout)
differential.why_considered: Acute monoarticular pain and swelling with warmth, often at the knee or elbow

history: Abrupt onset reaching peak intensity within hours
Severe pain even at rest, often waking the patient at night
Prior similar attacks or known crystal arthritis
Dietary triggers, alcohol, or diuretic use (gout)
exam: Intense joint-line tenderness with a tense effusion
Overlying erythema and warmth centered on the joint, not the bursa
Tophi or joint deformity in chronic gout
labs: Elevated uric acid (supportive but not diagnostic)
Synovial fluid with negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals (gout) or positively birefringent rhomboid crystals (pseudogout)
imaging: Joint effusion on ultrasound or x-ray
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges in chronic gout

differential.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
differential.why_considered: Joint pain and swelling, sometimes with a prominent periarticular component

history: Symmetrical small joint involvement of hands and wrists
Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Constitutional symptoms such as fatigue and low-grade fever
Family history of autoimmune disease
exam: Synovitis with boggy swelling of multiple joints
Joint-line tenderness and effusion
Rheumatoid nodules or hand deformities in established disease
labs: Positive rheumatoid factor or anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies
imaging: Symmetrical erosions and joint space narrowing on x-ray
Synovial proliferation and effusion on ultrasound or MRI

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Warm, red, swollen skin over a joint region, often confused with septic bursitis

history: Spreading redness and pain over the skin
Fever and chills
Recent skin break, wound, or fungal infection
exam: Diffuse erythema, warmth and induration of the skin without a discrete fluctuant bursal swelling
Lymphangitic streaking or regional lymphadenopathy
Tenderness of the skin and subcutaneous tissue rather than a focal bursa
labs: Blood cultures positive in severe cases
imaging: Ultrasound shows skin and subcutaneous thickening without a distended bursa
MRI shows soft tissue inflammation but no bursal fluid collection

differential.name: Tendinopathy or tendon tear
differential.why_considered: Focal periarticular pain and swelling worsened by movement, especially at the shoulder, elbow or heel

history: Pain localized to the tendon rather than the bursa
Pain with specific resisted movements
Overuse or repetitive activity
exam: Tenderness along the tendon course
Pain with resisted muscle contraction or passive stretch
Weakness or a palpable defect if torn
imaging: Ultrasound shows tendon thickening, hypoechoic change, or a tear
MRI shows tendon signal abnormality without a distended bursa

differential.name: Stress fracture
differential.why_considered: Activity-related focal bone pain with localized tenderness and swelling

history: Recent increase in repetitive weight-bearing activity
Pain worse with weight-bearing and relieved by rest
Night pain in some cases
exam: Focal bony tenderness rather than bursal tenderness
Pain with percussion or axial loading
imaging: X-ray may be normal early; periosteal reaction or fracture line later
MRI shows bone marrow edema and fracture line

severity.mild: Localized bursal pain and mild swelling, no warmth or fever, full range of motion with only end-range discomfort; responds to rest and ice
severity.moderate: Prominent swelling and tenderness, pain with most movement, mild warmth without systemic signs; limits work or activity
severity.severe: Marked swelling, warmth and pain with any movement, possible overlying erythema; raises concern for septic bursitis and warrants aspiration
severity.critical: Septic bursitis with systemic toxicity, spreading cellulitis, or sepsis; requires urgent aspiration, antibiotics and possible surgical drainage

red_flags.meaning: Suggests septic bursitis or another systemic infection; aspirate before injecting steroid

red_flags.finding: Marked warmth, spreading erythema or overlying cellulitis
red_flags.meaning: Concern for septic bursitis or soft tissue infection
Possible septic bursitis or hemorrhage; needs urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Open wound, draining sinus or recent penetrating injury over the bursa
Failure to improve after weeks of conservative care
red_flags.meaning: Reconsider the diagnosis or consider chronic bursitis requiring further workup

complications.name: Septic bursitis
clues: Marked warmth and erythema over the bursa

complications.name: Chronic or recurrent bursitis
clues: Recurrence with return to the offending activity

complications.name: Skin breakdown or sinus tract formation

special_populations.differences: May present with less swelling and more chronic pain, often attributed to osteoarthritis; slower recovery and higher risk of falls from knee pain.
Higher risk of septic bursitis and delayed healing; glycemic control should be optimized and infection ruled out early.
Higher risk of septic bursitis with atypical or muted inflammatory signs; lower threshold for aspiration and cultures.
Increased mechanical stress on weight-bearing joints; may have more diffuse pain and difficulty localizing to the bursa.
Bursitis is uncommon; consider trauma, infection, juvenile idiopathic arthritis and malignancy before attributing symptoms to bursitis.

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain, and can you point to it with one finger?
key_questions.looking_for: Well-localized pain over a bursa (prepatellar, olecranon, or other site) rather than diffuse joint or bone pain

key_questions.question: How did it start — did it come on gradually after activity, or suddenly?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days after repetitive activity or prolonged pressure; sudden severe onset raises concern for infection or crystal arthritis

key_questions.question: What makes the pain worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Kneeling, leaning on the elbow, direct pressure, or repetitive joint movement

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in aseptic bursitis; present suggests septic bursitis

key_questions.question: Have you had an injury, fall, or wound over that area recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent trauma or skin break, which raises the risk of septic bursitis

key_questions.question: Is the swelling getting better, worse, or staying the same?
key_questions.looking_for: Stable or improving with rest; rapidly enlarging swelling suggests infection or hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Does the joint ever lock, catch, or give way?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; mechanical symptoms suggest intra-articular pathology such as a meniscal tear

key_questions.question: Do you have pain or swelling in other joints?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; multiple joints suggest inflammatory arthritis or crystal disease

key_questions.question: What do you do for work or recreation — any repetitive kneeling, leaning on elbows, or overhead activity?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational or recreational overuse that fits the affected bursa

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, gout, rheumatoid arthritis, or any condition that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that raise the risk of septic bursitis or crystal arthritis

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including any steroids or immunosuppressants?
Have you tried anything for it, and did it help?
key_questions.looking_for: Response to rest, ice, or over-the-counter pain relievers

reasoning_points: Focal pain and swelling localized over a bursa rather than the joint line
Gradual onset after repetitive activity or prolonged pressure on the joint
Pain worse with direct pressure and movement, better with rest
No fever, chills, or systemic toxicity
No true joint-line tenderness, effusion, locking, or instability
Imaging shows soft tissue swelling without fracture or dislocation
Septic bursitis considered and excluded when infection is a concern

easy: Classic prepatellar or olecranon swelling after repetitive kneeling or elbow leaning
Well-localized bursal tenderness with no fever
Pain worse with pressure and movement, better with rest
X-ray shows soft tissue swelling only
medium: Older adult with chronic knee pain attributed to osteoarthritis
Patient with diabetes and mild warmth where septic bursitis must be excluded
Coexisting gout or rheumatoid arthritis confusing the picture
Deep bursitis (shoulder, hip) with less obvious swelling
hard: Septic bursitis with fever and overlying cellulitis mimicking aseptic bursitis
Atypical site such as the hip or heel with poorly localized pain
Immunocompromised patient with muted inflammatory signs
Chronic bursitis with fibrosis and persistent firm swelling
